> **Purpose of this document.** This is a draft motivation section for
> `ui_composition_benchmark.qmd`. The main report already contains an academic
> literature review (Section 2) covering the recipiency-decline puzzle
> (Burtless 1983; Blank and Card 1991; Anderson and Meyer 1997; Kuka and Stuart
> 2025; Lachowska, Sorkin, and Woodbury 2025). What that section does *not* do
> is explain why the question matters to the people who actually consume UI
> data in real time: Fed economists, Wall Street strategists, journalists, and
> policymakers who treat Thursday's claims print as a labor-market temperature
> check. This document fills that gap with a practitioner-oriented review of
> blog posts, news coverage, and policy commentary.
>
> **A note on links.** Where possible I link directly to the specific
> piece (Fed Economic Letter, think-tank report, blog post, or
> newsletter). Hub/landing-page URLs appear only when the reference is to
> an ongoing series (e.g., FEDS Notes as a venue) rather than a specific
> article. Paywalled outlets like Bloomberg, WSJ, and Reuters rotate and
> gate their URLs; for those I name authors and dates so the pieces can
> be located via site search even if a direct link rots.

# 1. Why UI Claims Became the Market's Favorite Labor Indicator

The U.S. Department of Labor releases initial and continued unemployment
insurance claims every Thursday at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, covering the week that
ended the previous Saturday for initial claims and the week before that for
continued claims. The release is posted at
[oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/claims.asp](https://oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/claims.asp)
and as a DOL news release at
[dol.gov/ui/data.pdf](https://www.dol.gov/ui/data.pdf). The two headline
series, ICSA and CCSA, are mirrored at FRED:
[fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ICSA](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ICSA) and
[fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CCSA](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CCSA).

Three features make claims unusually attractive as a real-time signal
relative to the monthly BLS employment situation release:

1. **Frequency.** Weekly, not monthly. In a turning-point environment, a
   monthly lag is an eternity.
2. **Timeliness.** Published with a five-day lag, versus the three-week lag
   on the BLS payroll report.
3. **Administrative grounding.** Claims are counted when people file, not
   estimated from a survey with a response rate that has fallen from the
   high-80s in the early 2010s to the low-70s in the 2020s (see the Census
   Bureau's CPS nonresponse documentation at
   [census.gov/programs-surveys/cps/technical-documentation](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/cps/technical-documentation.html)).

Because of these features, claims became the default "nowcast" input for
labor-market watchers long before high-frequency alternatives like Homebase,
Kronos/UKG, and ADP's research series existed. The Federal Reserve Bank of
St. Louis explains the role of claims as a leading indicator on its
*On the Economy* blog at
[stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy](https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy),
and FRED tags ICSA as a leading business-cycle indicator on its series page.

# 2. Claims, Flows, and the Unemployment Rate: An Accounting Primer

Before getting into how practitioners use claims, it helps to be explicit
about what the three headline objects — initial claims (ICSA), continued
claims (CCSA), and the unemployment rate — mechanically measure. Each
sits at a different point in the labor-market flow diagram, and their
relationships are not symmetric.

## 2.1 Initial claims: a firing-margin flow with an eligibility filter

ICSA is the weekly *inflow* into the insured-unemployment pool. Almost
every initial claim is filed because of a separation the filer did not
initiate — layoffs, plant closures, temporary furloughs, completed temp
contracts — because federal-state UI provides benefits only to workers
"unemployed through no fault of their own (as determined under state
law)" (U.S. Department of Labor, ["How Do I File for Unemployment
Insurance?"](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/unemployment-insurance)).
Two gaps on either side of that mapping:

- **Fires that don't generate claims.** The unemployed person must
  satisfy monetary eligibility (sufficient base-period covered earnings),
  be able and available for work, be actively seeking work, and not have
  been discharged for misconduct. Long-tenured workers at covered
  employers clear these bars easily; short-tenure workers, part-timers,
  and gig/1099 workers often do not. State-by-state rules for each of
  these requirements are catalogued in DOL ETA's ["Comparison of State
  Unemployment Insurance Laws,
  2023"](https://oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/comparison/2020-2029/comparison2023.asp)
  (see especially the chapters on *Monetary Entitlement* and *Nonmonetary
  Eligibility*). The size of this gap is exactly the ineligible share of
  the unemployed — the composition variable this report focuses on.
- **Non-fires that do generate claims.** Most quits are denied (job
  leavers fail the "through no fault of own" test), but certain
  "good-cause" quits qualify in some states. The *Nonmonetary
  Eligibility* chapter of the DOL Comparison catalogues state rules on
  good-cause exceptions including domestic violence, spousal relocation,
  health reasons, and (in a subset of states) good cause not attributable
  to the employer.

So ICSA is a noisy, undercounted read on firings, where the undercount
moves with who the unemployed are.

## 2.2 Continued claims: a stock that picks up hiring only indirectly

CCSA is the *stock* of people currently drawing benefits. The accounting
identity is:

$$
\text{CCSA}_t \;=\; \text{CCSA}_{t-1} + \text{ICSA}_t - \text{exits}_t
$$

Exits happen for three reasons: (i) find a job (the hiring margin); (ii)
exhaust benefits (duration caps, which range from 12 weeks in Florida,
Kentucky, and North Carolina to 30 weeks in Massachusetts under current
state laws, per the Congressional Research Service report ["Unemployment
Insurance: Programs and
Benefits"](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RL33362)); (iii) lose
continuing eligibility — failing the weekly able-and-available, active
work-search, or earnings-reporting requirements documented in the
*Continued Eligibility* section of the DOL ["Comparison of State
Unemployment Insurance Laws,
2023"](https://oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/comparison/2020-2029/comparison2023.asp),
or leaving the labor force entirely. Holding ICSA fixed, weaker hiring →
slower exits → higher CCSA. That is why practitioners read *rising CCSA
alongside stable ICSA* as a classic "hiring is weakening" signal, and
why the new Chicago Fed Labor Market Indicators explicitly split this
blended object into a separate separations rate and a hiring rate for
the unemployed (see §5.3).

## 2.3 The unemployment rate: mostly a hiring-margin object

The canonical steady-state approximation (Shimer 2005, 2012; Hall 2005)
is:

$$
u^* \;\approx\; \frac{s}{s+f}
$$

where $s$ is the separation rate into unemployment and $f$ is the
job-finding rate out of unemployment. Decomposing the cyclical variance
of $u$ into contributions from $s$ and $f$:

- **Shimer (2005, 2012):** roughly 75% from $f$, 25% from $s$.
- **Elsby–Michaels–Solon (2009), Fujita–Ramey (2009):** $s$ matters more
  at turning points and in deep recessions than Shimer's long-sample
  estimate suggests; closer to 60/40 at business-cycle frequencies.
- **Qualitative consensus:** in mild cycles $f$ dominates; in deep
  recessions both move, with $s$ contributing an early spike and $f$
  dominating the slow recovery.

David Wiczer's 2014 St. Louis Fed *On the Economy* piece ["The Issues
with New Unemployment Insurance Claims as a Labor Market
Indicator"](https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2014/september/the-issues-with-new-unemployment-insurance-claims-as-a-labor-market-indicator)
is the earliest practitioner-facing restatement of this point: 75–80% of
unemployment-rate movement comes from the job-finding rate, so a
series that reads the separation rate is inherently a weak predictor of
the unemployment rate.

## 2.4 Why the claims-to-unemployment mapping is inherently unstable

Putting the three objects together:

| Object | Primary driver | What it misses |
|---|---|---|
| ICSA | eligible fires | ineligible fires (the composition gap); hiring |
| CCSA | insured-unemployment stock | uninsured unemployed; picks up hiring only indirectly |
| Unemployment rate | mostly hiring (job-finding); separations second | — |

Because the unemployment rate is *predominantly* a hiring-margin object
while ICSA is *primarily* a firing-margin object, there is no mechanical
reason for the two to move together in a stable way. Two distinct
channels can drive them apart:

1. **Flow composition drift (the Shimer/Wiczer channel).** Shifts in the
   share of unemployment-rate variation coming from $s$ versus $f$
   automatically change the co-movement between claims (which read $s$)
   and the unemployment rate. Low-churn "low-hire, low-fire" regimes —
   the 2014 environment Wiczer flagged, and the 2023–2024 environment
   Bunker, Berger, and CFLMI document — are the canonical example.
2. **Stock composition drift (the channel this report focuses on).**
   Even holding $s$ and $f$ fixed, if the mix of the unemployed shifts
   toward groups that do not generate claims (job leavers, new entrants,
   reentrants, and the administratively ineligible), ICSA undercounts
   the firing margin by an amount that varies over time.

The practitioner literature reviewed below engages with both channels
informally. The composition benchmark formalizes channel (2), holding
channel (1) fixed by construction.

# 3. Claims in Recession Calls and Turning-Point Debates

## 3.1 The 2008–2009 recession

During the Great Recession, claims were the indicator journalists used to
communicate labor-market deterioration in real time because payroll
revisions were arriving months after the fact. The Brookings Institution's
Hamilton Project tracked claims alongside payrolls in its recession coverage;
its economic-indicators hub is at
[hamiltonproject.org](https://www.hamiltonproject.org/). Contemporary
coverage in The New York Times' Economix blog and at Calculated Risk
([calculatedriskblog.com](https://www.calculatedriskblog.com/)) treated the
Thursday claims release as the most important weekly data point of 2008–2009.
Calculated Risk in particular popularized the four-week moving average of
ICSA as a smoothing device, and the "break above 400K" threshold as a
shorthand for recession-consistent claims levels — a rule of thumb that
circulated through Bloomberg and WSJ commentary for years afterward.

## 3.2 The 2020 pandemic shock

In the pandemic, claims became the dominant labor-market story for roughly
six weeks in March and April 2020 because they updated in real time while
the April payroll report did not arrive until May 8. The week-ending
March 21, 2020 release of 3.28 million initial claims, followed by 6.87
million the following week, was the single most-cited economic data point
of the early pandemic and appeared on the front page of essentially every
major U.S. newspaper. Fed research published several pieces in 2020–2022
analyzing the divergence between claims and household-survey unemployment
— a divergence the present report argues is partly about composition. The
San Francisco Fed's *Economic Letter* ["Unemployment Insurance
Withdrawal"](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2022/04/unemployment-insurance-withdrawal/)
(Petrosky-Nadeau and Valletta, April 2022) compared hiring in states that
ended enhanced UI early against those that did not. More recently, the SF
Fed's ["Tracking Labor Market
Stress"](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2025/08/tracking-labor-market-stress/)
(Garimella, Jordà, and Singh, August 2025) builds a state-level claims-based
stress indicator and explicitly discusses the July 2024 "false alarm" in
which national aggregates overstated stress that remained geographically
concentrated — directly relevant framing for the state-panel approach of
this report.

The pandemic episode also exposed the limits of claims as a
denominator-free indicator. The enormous PUA (Pandemic Unemployment
Assistance) program temporarily extended coverage to gig workers and the
self-employed, groups normally excluded from ICSA. Andrew Stettner's
Century Foundation report ["A Pandemic Lifeline: Nation's Unemployment
System Is Inadequate and Unprepared for Next
Downturn"](https://tcf.org/content/report/a-pandemic-lifeline-nations-unemployment-system-is-inadequate-and-unprepared-for-next-downturn/)
and ["Unemployment Trust Fund Recovery Is Helping Employers, not
Workers"](https://tcf.org/content/report/unemployment-trust-fund-recovery-helping-employers-not-workers/)
document why regular-program claims behaved strangely during 2020–2021 and
why the system entered the post-pandemic period structurally thinner than
official recipiency rates suggested.

## 3.3 The 2023–2024 soft-landing debate

The most recent and most relevant episode for the present report is the
soft-landing debate of 2023 through early 2025. Throughout this period,
initial claims stayed historically low — typically 200K to 240K per week —
while the unemployment rate drifted up from 3.4 percent in April 2023 to
4.2 percent by mid-2024. This divergence is exactly the kind of
claims-intensity gap that the composition benchmark is designed to
characterize.

Key commentators who wrote repeatedly about this tension, with
representative pieces:

- **Claudia Sahm**, *Stay-At-Home Macro*. Sahm is the inventor of the Sahm
  Rule recession indicator (documented at the FRED series page
  [SAHMREALTIME](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SAHMREALTIME); she
  walks through the construction in ["The Sahm rule: step by
  step"](https://stayathomemacro.substack.com/p/the-sahm-rule-step-by-step)).
  On the 2024 trigger, see ["The Sahm rule: I created a
  monster"](https://stayathomemacro.substack.com/p/the-sahm-rule-i-created-a-monster)
  — her own argument that the rule is *overstating* weakness because the
  2024 rise in unemployment was being driven by labor-force entry and
  reentry rather than layoffs, which do not generate UI claims. ["A Year
  With No Jobs—But No
  Recession"](https://stayathomemacro.substack.com/p/a-year-with-no-jobsbut-no-recession)
  develops the broader soft-landing-plus-weak-hiring story.
- **Nick Bunker**, Indeed Hiring Lab. See Bunker's ["January 2024 JOLTS
  Statement: Quitting is Slowing
  Down"](https://www.hiringlab.org/2024/03/06/january-2024-jolts-statement/)
  and ["July 2024 Labor Market
  Update"](https://www.hiringlab.org/2024/07/11/july-labor-market-update-slowdown-posted-wage-growth/),
  both of which characterize the 2024 environment as one where both
  hiring and separations have fallen to pre-pandemic or below-pre-pandemic
  levels — the "low-hire, low-fire" pattern that is also now the organizing
  frame of the new Chicago Fed Labor Market Indicators (see §4.3).
- **Guy Berger**, Burning Glass Institute (previously LinkedIn Economic
  Graph). See the ["Labor Market Outlook August
  2024"](https://www.burningglassinstitute.org/research/labor-market-outlook-august-2024)
  and Berger's interview coverage of ["The Great
  Stay"](https://www.housingwire.com/articles/burning-glass-institutes-guy-berger-explores-the-great-stay-in-the-labor-and-housing-markets/),
  in which he stresses the historically low rate of involuntary
  separations as the defining feature of the 2024 labor market — a near
  restatement of this report's composition story.
- **Ernie Tedeschi**, Yale Budget Lab (formerly CEA Chief Economist). The
  most directly relevant piece is the accounting exercise ["Immigration
  and the U.S. Economy Since the
  Pandemic"](https://www.briefingbook.info/p/immigration-and-the-us-economy-since),
  which decomposes post-2019 labor-supply growth into direct and
  unemployment-rate effects of immigration. See also the Georgetown
  FinPolicy talk ["Looking Back on the US Economy in 2024 and its Outlook
  for
  2025"](https://finpolicy.georgetown.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/US-Economy-in-2024-and-2025.pdf).
- **Jed Kolko**, formerly Commerce Department chief economist. See ["No,
  Native-Born Employment Has Not
  Soared"](https://jedkolko.substack.com/p/no-native-born-employment-has-not)
  on native-vs-foreign-born unemployment divergence, and ["Can new data
  solve an immigration
  puzzle?"](https://www.slowboring.com/p/can-new-data-solve-an-immigration)
  on the census-vs-CBO immigration measurement gap that shaped
  labor-market nowcasts in 2024.
- **Heidi Shierholz**, Economic Policy Institute. See ["Assessing the
  strength of the labor market"
  (EPI, 2024)](https://www.epi.org/blog/assessing-the-strength-of-the-labor-market-preliminary-downward-revisions-do-not-necessarily-signal-a-weaker-2024-labor-market-but-there-are-warning-signs-for-2025/),
  which argues that preliminary payroll revisions do not imply a weaker
  2024 labor market but flags warning signs for 2025.
- **Arindrajit Dube** and others writing at the Washington Center for
  [Equitable Growth](https://equitablegrowth.org/) have made related
  arguments about composition, recipiency, and labor-market slack.

# 4. Claims as a Recession Indicator: Rules of Thumb

Three rules of thumb for reading claims as a labor-market signal circulate
widely in the financial and policy press. All three are relevant to the
composition benchmark because all three implicitly assume a stable mapping
from claims to unemployment, which the present report documents has
weakened.

## 4.1 The four-week moving average and the "400K line"

Weekly initial claims are genuinely noisy. Three sources of week-to-week
variation make the raw series hard to read in real time:

1. **Fixed-week holiday effects.** Thanksgiving, Christmas/New Year's,
   Independence Day, and Memorial Day shift the number of filing days in
   the reference week and change the timing of when people file; the BLS
   seasonal adjustment handles the typical calendar pattern but not
   timing quirks like years when a holiday falls midweek. The DOL release
   itself reports both the weekly seasonally-adjusted level and the
   four-week moving average for exactly this reason (see the standing
   release template at
   [dol.gov/ui/data.pdf](https://www.dol.gov/ui/data.pdf) and FRED series
   [IC4WSA](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IC4WSA)).
2. **Weather and one-off shocks.** Hurricanes, winter storms, auto-plant
   retooling weeks, and government shutdowns can move a single weekly
   print by 20,000–100,000 without any underlying change in labor-market
   conditions. The four-week average attenuates these one-off events.
3. **Seasonal-adjustment difficulty at weekly frequency.** UI claims are
   among the hardest official series to seasonally adjust because the
   seasonal factors are estimated from short weekly windows and the
   underlying seasonal pattern has shifted as industries (construction,
   retail hiring) have restructured. Multiplicative seasonal factors at
   holiday weeks are especially unstable.

Averaging four consecutive weeks of the seasonally-adjusted series
suppresses these sources of noise while preserving the underlying
persistent movements a labor-market analyst is trying to read. Crucially,
because each Thursday release publishes the *prior* week's claims, the
four-week moving average is only five weeks stale at most — still faster
than monthly payrolls — so the smoothing trades a modest amount of
timeliness for a large reduction in sampling-style noise.

Overlaid on this smoothing convention, the rule of thumb that a
four-week-average ICSA above roughly 400K (in a labor force of ~160M) is
recession-consistent dates at least to the 1990s. Calculated Risk
([calculatedriskblog.com](https://www.calculatedriskblog.com/)) maintained
running commentary on this threshold through every cycle from 2008 to
present. The rule is crude but historically effective — until 2023, when
claims stayed well below 250K while the unemployment rate climbed. That
breakdown is the motivation for the composition-adjusted benchmark.

## 4.2 The Sahm Rule

Claudia Sahm's recession indicator (FRED series
[SAHMREALTIME](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SAHMREALTIME)) is not a
claims rule per se — it uses the unemployment rate — but it is often
discussed in the same breath as claims because both are framed as
real-time recession signals. Sahm's own self-contained explainer of how
the rule is constructed is ["The Sahm rule: step by
step"](https://stayathomemacro.substack.com/p/the-sahm-rule-step-by-step).
(The rule was originally introduced in a 2019 Hamilton Project chapter on
automatic stabilizers as a trigger for direct stimulus payments; the
chapter itself is about fiscal stabilization policy, not about the rule
as a standalone recession signal, so it is not the natural primary
citation for the indicator.)

In July 2024 the Sahm Rule triggered while claims remained benign. The
resulting commentary leaned heavily on the distinction between "bad
unemployment" (layoffs, which claims capture) and "good unemployment"
(entry and reentry, which claims miss) — exactly the
job-separations-versus-labor-force-entry split that organizes the
present report. Sahm's own response to the trigger (["The Sahm rule: I
created a
monster"](https://stayathomemacro.substack.com/p/the-sahm-rule-i-created-a-monster))
argued that the rule was overstating weakness precisely because the
composition of the unemployment rise was anomalous.

## 4.3 Continued claims and duration

Continued claims (CCSA) are more closely tied to the duration of
unemployment spells and are often read as a leading indicator of hiring
weakness rather than firing strength. The Richmond Fed's *Economic Brief*
series at
[richmondfed.org/publications/research/economic_brief](https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/economic_brief)
and the Kansas City Fed's *Macro Bulletin* have repeatedly used continued
claims in this way. During 2023–2024, continued claims rose modestly while
initial claims stayed low, and practitioner commentary read this as
evidence that hiring was weakening even as layoffs were not rising — again
consistent with the composition story.

# 5. The "Claims as Proxy" Skeptics

Not all practitioners accept claims at face value. A parallel strand of
commentary has argued for years that claims are an increasingly
unrepresentative proxy for labor-market health, and this strand is the
natural audience for the composition benchmark.

## 5.1 The shrinking recipiency rate

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities has published repeatedly on
the long-run decline in UI recipiency and the policy implications. See
Chad Stone and William Chen, ["Introduction to Unemployment
Insurance"](https://www.cbpp.org/research/introduction-to-unemployment-insurance),
and CBPP's ["Key Things to Know About Unemployment
Insurance"](https://www.cbpp.org/research/key-things-to-know-about-unemployment-insurance)
and state-level data piece ["Unemployment Insurance Recipiency Rates by
State,
2022"](https://www.cbpp.org/media/unemployment-insurance-recipiency-rates-by-state-2022).
The through-line: recipiency has fallen from roughly 50 percent in the
1950s to near 25 percent immediately before the pandemic, which means
claims understate labor-market distress because an increasing share of
the unemployed are not eligible for benefits.

The Urban Institute's most-cited technical reference on this is Wayne
Vroman's ["Low Benefit Recipiency in State Unemployment Insurance
Programs"](https://www.urban.org/research/publication/low-benefit-recipiency-state-unemployment-insurance-programs),
a DOL-commissioned study that decomposes state-level recipiency variation
into labor-market and program-administration components — directly the
question the residual of this report's composition benchmark is designed
to address. See also Urban's overview ["An Introduction to Unemployment
and Unemployment
Insurance"](https://www.urban.org/research/publication/introduction-unemployment-and-unemployment-insurance).

The Century Foundation's work is anchored by Andrew Stettner. In addition
to the pandemic pieces cited in §2.2, see ["Our Unemployment System
Needs Modernizing"](https://tcf.org/content/report/our-unemployment-system-needs-modernizing-trump-is-doing-the-opposite/)
and the ongoing ["Unemployment Insurance Data
Dashboard"](https://tcf.org/content/report/unemployment-insurance-data-dashboard/),
which tracks state-level recipiency in real time.

The National Employment Law Project's flagship recipiency report is
["Closing Doors on the Unemployed: Why Most Jobless Workers Are Not
Receiving Unemployment
Insurance"](https://www.nelp.org/insights-research/closing-doors-on-the-unemployed/).
See also ["Ten Years After Great Recession Hit, Unemployed Workers Face
Greater Barriers to Jobless
Aid"](https://www.nelp.org/ten-years-after-great-recession-hit-unemployed-workers-face-greater-barriers-to-jobless-aid/)
and NELP's ongoing ["Unemployment
Insurance"](https://www.nelp.org/explore-the-issues/unemployment-insurance/)
issue hub, which documents the eligibility restrictions, benefit-week
cuts, and procedural hurdles that drive the non-composition part of the
recipiency story.

## 5.2 The composition critique in financial commentary

On the financial-commentary side, Joseph Brusuelas at RSM has been the
most consistent voice on the labor-supply-driven unemployment rise. See
his RSM *Real Economy* pieces ["Market Minute: The declining labor
supply, the jobless rate and Fed
policy"](https://realeconomy.rsmus.com/market-minute-the-declining-labor-supply-the-jobless-rate-and-fed-policy/)
and ["U.S. August jobs report: A soft landing in the
economy"](https://realeconomy.rsmus.com/u-s-august-jobs-report-a-soft-landing-in-the-economy/),
both of which attribute the 2024 rise in the unemployment rate to
immigration-driven labor-force expansion against historically low
layoffs.

Mark Zandi of Moody's Analytics made the same diagnosis in 2024 —
unemployment "ticked up despite job creation because labor force growth
is booming" (quoted in CNBC's ["Immigration is taking pressure off the
job market"](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/03/02/immigration-taking-pressure-off-the-job-market-us-economy-expert.html)).
By 2026 Zandi's Vicious Cycle Index (see Axios, ["A new recession red
flag"](https://www.axios.com/2026/04/08/jobs-recession-index-zandi))
inverted that framing for the post-immigration-slowdown period —
illustrating exactly why a benchmark that holds composition fixed is
useful across both regimes.

These pieces are representative rather than exhaustive; the bank, ratings,
and consultancy research desks covered the same themes throughout
2023–2024, often behind client paywalls but routinely quoted in Bloomberg,
Reuters, and WSJ coverage.

## 5.3 Fed commentary

Fed research publications have been more circumspect but cover the same
ground. The directly relevant specific pieces:

- **San Francisco Fed.** Garimella, Jordà, and Singh, ["Tracking Labor
  Market
  Stress"](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2025/08/tracking-labor-market-stress/)
  (August 2025) constructs a state-level claims-based stress indicator
  and walks through the July 2024 false alarm in detail. Petrosky-Nadeau
  and Valletta, ["Unemployment Insurance
  Withdrawal"](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2022/04/unemployment-insurance-withdrawal/)
  (April 2022), quantifies hiring effects of early withdrawal from
  enhanced pandemic UI. See also the more recent ["Recent Slowdown in
  Labor Supply and
  Demand"](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2026/01/recent-slowdown-in-labor-supply-and-demand/)
  (January 2026).
- **Cleveland Fed.** ["Immigration and the Unemployment Rate in
  2023–2024"](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2026/ec-202605-immigration-and-unemployment-rate-2023-2024)
  is the most direct Fed decomposition of the supply-side story in the
  soft-landing window.
- **Chicago Fed.** Two pieces are directly relevant here. First, the
  methodological antecedent: Brave, Butters, and Kelley, ["A 'Big Data'
  View of the U.S. Economy: Introducing the Brave-Butters-Kelley
  Indexes"](https://www.chicagofed.org/publications/chicago-fed-letter/2019/422)
  (*Chicago Fed Letter* 422, 2019). Second — and squarely on the same
  terrain as this report — the Chicago Fed launched the ["Chicago Fed
  Labor Market
  Indicators"](https://www.chicagofed.org/research/data/chicago-fed-labor-market-indicators/latest-release)
  (CFLMI) in September 2025, documented in ["Introducing the Chicago Fed
  Labor Market
  Indicators"](https://www.chicagofed.org/publications/chicago-fed-insights/2025/introducing-chicago-fed-labor-market-indicators)
  and extended in ["A Closer Look at the Low-Hire, Low-Fire Labor Market
  with the Chicago Fed Labor Market
  Indicators"](https://www.chicagofed.org/publications/chicago-fed-insights/2026/low-hire-low-fire-chicago-fed-labor-market-indicators).
  CFLMI publishes a layoffs/other-separations rate, a hiring rate for the
  unemployed, and a forecast of the monthly BLS unemployment rate, and
  uses official UI claims as one of its real-time inputs. That makes it a
  natural downstream consumer of the composition-adjusted claims series
  that this report builds: substituting the composition-benchmark-implied
  claims for the official series in CFLMI isolates the counterfactual
  unemployment rate, separations rate, and hiring rate one would read if
  claims tracked the compositional mix of the unemployed alone.
- **Board of Governors** [FEDS
  Notes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/default.htm).
- Kansas City Fed [*Economic
  Review*](https://www.kansascityfed.org/research/economic-review/) and
  Richmond Fed [*Economic
  Brief*](https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/economic_brief)
  cover related topics on slack, participation, and duration.

# 6. Why This Matters for the Composition Benchmark

The practitioner literature above converges on a claim that the
composition benchmark in `ui_composition_benchmark.qmd` makes precise:

> **Weekly UI claims are a cleaner signal of labor-market health when the
> unemployed population looks like the population UI was designed for — i.e.,
> job losers with prior covered earnings — than when it is tilted toward
> entrants, reentrants, and job leavers.**

Every commentator cited above makes some version of this argument
informally. None quantifies it in a reduced-form panel. That is the
contribution of the present report, and the practitioner literature is
the audience that would most directly benefit from it. Specifically:

1. **Market economists** who publish weekly Thursday claims commentary
   need a composition-adjusted benchmark to say whether a given claims
   reading is "low" relative to the current mix of unemployment, not just
   relative to history.
2. **Fed research staff** modeling labor-market slack need a way to
   reconcile claims and household-survey unemployment when they
   diverge — composition is one of the top candidate explanations.
3. **Policy analysts at CBPP, TCF, NELP, Urban, and the Hamilton Project**
   arguing for UI reform need empirical evidence on how much of the
   recipiency decline is mechanical (composition) versus policy
   (administrative burden, tax treatment, state choices). The benchmark's
   residual is precisely the non-compositional part they care about.
4. **Journalists** writing the Thursday-morning claims story need a
   framework for explaining why a 220K print in 2024 does not mean the
   same thing as a 220K print in 2004. Composition is the simplest
   explanation and the one that maps most cleanly onto the
   soft-landing narrative of 2023–2024.

# 7. Suggested Placement in the Main Report

I would slot a condensed version of this material into
`ui_composition_benchmark.qmd` as a new **Section 1.1 ("Why UI claims are
watched")** immediately after the introduction, and reference specific
practitioner pieces inline in the existing Section 2 literature review to
give it a blog-and-news companion to its academic citations. The current
Section 2 should remain the rigorous academic review; this new material is
explicitly labeled as practitioner context and should not displace it.

A two-paragraph compressed version that could live in Section 1.1:

> *Initial and continued UI claims are the most closely watched weekly
> labor-market indicator in U.S. financial markets and economic journalism.
> The Thursday claims release at 8:30 a.m. Eastern moves Treasury yields,
> generates front-page coverage in downturns, and is the standard input to
> real-time recession calls, including the "400K line" rule of thumb
> popularized on Calculated Risk and the Sahm Rule that triggered in July
> 2024. During the 2023–2024 soft-landing debate, practitioners including
> Claudia Sahm (*Stay-At-Home Macro*), Nick Bunker (Indeed Hiring Lab),
> Guy Berger (Burning Glass Institute), Ernie Tedeschi (Yale Budget Lab),
> and Jed Kolko repeatedly flagged a divergence: claims stayed low while
> the unemployment rate drifted up, and the standard interpretation was
> that the rise in unemployment was being driven by labor-force entry and
> reentry rather than layoffs.*
>
> *That practitioner consensus is informally a composition story: claims
> track the job-losing unemployed, and when unemployment is tilted toward
> entrants, reentrants, and job leavers, claims understate distress in the
> sense of missing non-claimant unemployment but also accurately capture
> the smaller claimant-relevant subset. What the practitioner literature
> has not done is quantify this mapping. This report fills that gap by
> estimating a reduced-form composition benchmark for claims intensity in
> an annual state panel, then characterizing the residual gap between
> observed and benchmark-predicted intensity — the portion that
> composition cannot explain and that institutional and administrative
> factors must.*

# 9. Open Questions for the Main Report

Four gaps in the practitioner literature that the composition benchmark
could explicitly address, and that would sharpen the main report's
positioning:

1. **How much of the 2023–2024 claims-unemployment divergence is
   composition?** Sahm, Bunker, and Tedeschi all asserted it was "a lot"
   but none produced a decomposition. The state-panel regressions in
   Section 7 of the main report are well positioned to answer this
   quantitatively.
2. **Does the composition channel operate symmetrically in downturns and
   recoveries?** The practitioner consensus implicitly assumes it does,
   but the residual term $\varepsilon_{st}$ in the benchmark specification
   may behave asymmetrically — this would be a direct empirical
   contribution.
3. **Is the state panel's composition-adjusted residual correlated with
   the administrative-burden measures that the CBPP/TCF/NELP literature
   emphasizes?** This is the natural bridge between the composition story
   (which this report quantifies) and the institutional story (which the
   policy literature documents qualitatively). A correlation result would
   give the main report a direct policy-literature hook.
4. **What does a composition-only claims series imply when plugged into
   the Chicago Fed Labor Market Indicators?** CFLMI (launched September
   2025) forecasts the BLS unemployment rate, a layoffs/other-separations
   rate, and a hiring rate for the unemployed using official UI claims as
   a real-time input. Replacing the actual CC/CE series with the
   composition-benchmark prediction isolates the counterfactual readings
   one would see if claims tracked the compositional mix of the
   unemployed alone — i.e., the part of the CFLMI signal that is
   *mechanical* given who is unemployed, separated from the part driven
   by administrative frictions, employer behavior, and state-program
   design. No other piece in the practitioner literature does this
   substitution, and it is the most direct way to translate the report's
   reduced-form result into an object Fed and market watchers already
   read.
